summary: The note defines energy demand as the consumption of energy by human activity, which shapes total energy use, fuel supply location and types, and end-use technologies. It argues the UK must eliminate fossil fuels from its energy system by 2050 to respond to climate change, since efficiency alone is insufficient. It discusses renewables integration challenges, demand-side flexibility and storage, decarbonising heating and transport with electrification and hydrogen, and outlines how the CREDS programme divides energy demand research into sectoral and cross-cutting themes.
one_line: Explains energy demand as human energy consumption and argues the UK must eliminate fossil fuels by 2050 through efficiency, renewables, flexibility and decarbonised heating and transport.
key_facts: Energy demand is the term used to describe the consumption of energy by human activity.
Energy demand drives the total amount of energy used, the location and types of fuel used in the energy supply system, and the characteristics of end use technologies.
When discussing energy demand, all uses of energy are referred to: electricity, transport fuels, and fuels for heating and industrial processes.
To respond to the threat of climate change, the UK will need to eliminate fossil fuels from its energy system by 2050.
Energy efficiency has increased and demand in the UK has fallen significantly in the last decade.
Improved energy efficiency is critical but will not be sufficient; the UK will also need to move away from fossil fuels.
The costs of wind and solar energy are falling rapidly, leading to higher proportions of renewables in electricity generation.
Solar and wind are variable sources, which makes balancing electricity supply and demand more difficult.
Demand side response involves changing energy practices (e.g. doing the washing at different times) or storing energy locally (e.g. in hot water tanks or electric vehicle batteries).
Smart devices connected via the internet and smart meters to a smart grid are technologies that promise to manage demand.
Complete electrification of heating is unlikely, so new energy carriers such as hydrogen will likely be needed.
Moving away from fossil fuels in freight transport, aviation, shipping and many industrial processes raises similar issues to heating.
In CREDS, energy demand study was divided into three sectoral areas: transport, buildings, and materials.
CREDS supplements its sectoral areas with three cross-cutting themes: flexibility, digital, and policy.
